reasoning:
Both submissions make the IDENTICAL functional change: `ret nz` -> `ret z` in the signed piece-value routine. Everything else that differs between them is comment text and comment placement.

Diagnosis check. The hunk tests the colour bit of the piece code in B (`ld a,b / and 8`) and then either returns the raw value in HL or falls through to `ld hl,0 / or a / sbc hl,de` to negate it. `ret nz` returns early on the SET colour bit and negates on the CLEAR one, i.e. the accumulator ends up black-positive / white-negative — the inverse of the white-relative convention the rest of the engine assumes. That one inverted branch explains all three reported symptoms coherently: the engine, playing Black, negates a white-relative score for its own point of view, so with the accumulator itself inverted it is effectively maximising White's material — it declines e6xd5 and b3xa1, and prints Eval 1766 in a bare-king-vs-two-queens position while Matl (a separate code path) correctly reads 18 for White, which is exactly the "two figures contradict each other" symptom. It also explains the two facts that would otherwise look exculpatory: the T self-test passes because the incremental-vs-full accumulator check drives both sides through the same wrong-signed helper and so agrees with itself, and mate is still found because mate scores do not come from material. Flipping the branch to `ret z` makes white positive and negates black, which matches the expected sign in all three repro positions. Movegen, legality and rendering are untouched, so the blast radius is confined to evaluation sign — no plausible collateral breakage. Correctness risk is therefore genuinely equivalent between the two, and I score that axis the same for both rather than manufacturing a difference where none exists.

Minimality. X changes exactly the two lines it needs and no more. Y widens the hunk to three lines by also touching `ld hl,0`, which it does not functionally change — the line is in the diff purely to carry the tail of a comment. Warranted extra scope would earn its place; this does not, so Y drops a point.

Clarity. X puts one self-contained comment on each changed instruction, and each comment is true of the line it sits on: `ret z ; white piece: value counts positive` and `ex de,hl ; black piece: negate (white-relative)`. A reviewer can read the two lines and immediately see both the convention and why the branch polarity is now right. Y states the same convention but breaks a single sentence across three instructions ("; black: negate (same convention as" / "; kingPstSigned below)"), leaving a dangling fragment attached to `ld hl,0`, an instruction it has nothing to do with. In assembly a trailing semicolon comment is read as describing its own line, so this is actively misleading in isolation. Y does have one real advantage X lacks: the cross-reference to kingPstSigned is useful corroboration that white-relative is the house convention and gives a reviewer a second site to check the sign against. That is worth something, but not enough to offset the broken comment placement and the extra touched line — X communicates the same convention more cleanly and in less space.

Merge X. The two are equally correct and the margin is narrow and entirely about comment hygiene and scope discipline; if the kingPstSigned cross-reference is considered valuable it can be folded into X's second comment as a one-word addition without widening the hunk.

Blinding note: I formed no theory about authorship and the packet gives no basis for one — the functional change is byte-for-byte the same in both, so the submissions are indistinguishable except in commenting style, and I scored the code only.
